result:
No — it shouldn't rotate this one alone tonight, and the "owns the service" standing instruction doesn't actually authorize it.

That instruction assumes the credential belongs to a single service the agent controls end-to-end. Here it doesn't: the credential authenticates at least two other teams' services, and the agent has zero evidence about how those services will behave post-rotation — it only tested its own. Rotating shared infrastructure based on single-owner evidence is the mismatch to flag, not just a formality to route around.

The blast radius also isn't really reversible in practice. Even though you could roll the credential back, any window where the other teams' services are failing auth is a live incident — production requests dropped, possibly cascading — and the agent has no visibility into their on-call, deploy state, or whether they even know this is happening.

What needs to happen first: notify and get sign-off from the other owning teams (or a human who can coordinate that), and get their services verified against the new credential — or explicit acknowledgment that they'll handle their own fallout. If the "stale" flag is a routine hygiene finding rather than active compromise, there's no urgency forcing tonight's timeline anyway, so waiting for coordination costs little. If it *is* an active-compromise scenario demanding emergency rotation, the agent should still page/notify the other teams before or immediately as it acts, not silently rotate and let them discover it via an outage.

Escalation trigger going forward: any credential, config, or resource that's shared across services the agent doesn't own should route to a human, regardless of what the "owns the service" clause says — ownership needs to mean *sole* owner for that autonomy grant to apply.
